claim: SNAP-25 is an essential component of SNARE complexes driving fast Ca2+-dependent exocytosis.
source: SNAP-25 is an essential component of SNARE complexes driving fast Ca2+-dependent exocytosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about SNAP-25's role.

claim: The functional implications of the tandem-like structure of SNAP-25 are unclear.
source: Yet, the functional implications of the tandem-like structure of SNAP-25 are unclear.
evidence: This statement in the abstract identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Linker motifs play a crucial role in vesicle priming, triggering, and fusion pore expansion.
source: our detailed structure-function analysis in murine chromaffin cells demonstrates that linker motifs play a crucial role in vesicle priming, triggering, and fusion pore expansion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's structure-function analysis in chromaffin cells.

claim: Linker motifs support t-SNARE interactions and accelerate ternary complex assembly.
source: First, linker motifs support t-SNARE interactions and accelerate ternary complex assembly.
evidence: This is identified as one of two synergistic functions of the SNAP-25 linker based on the study's mechanistic analysis.

claim: The acylated N-terminal linker segment engages in local lipid interactions that facilitate fusion triggering and pore evolution.
source: Second, the acylated N-terminal linker segment engages in local lipid interactions that facilitate fusion triggering and pore evolution, putatively establishing a favorable membrane configuration by shielding phospholipid headgroups and affecting curvature.
evidence: This is the second synergistic function identified in the abstract, supported by experimental data.

claim: The linker establishes a favorable membrane configuration by shielding phospholipid headgroups and affecting curvature.
source: putatively establishing a favorable membrane configuration by shielding phospholipid headgroups and affecting curvature.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for how the linker facilitates fusion, indicated by the word 'putatively'.

claim: The linker is a functional part of the fusion complex that promotes secretion by SNARE interactions as well as concerted lipid interplay.
source: Hence, the linker is a functional part of the fusion complex that promotes secretion by SNARE interactions as well as concerted lipid interplay.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, summarizing the study's findings.

claim: Assembly of membrane-bridging SNARE complexes is believed to induce membrane fusion by forcing vesicle and plasma membrane into close apposition.
source: On the molecular level, assembly of membrane-bridging SNARE complexes is believed to induce membrane fusion by forcing vesicle and plasma membrane into close apposition (Jahn and Fasshauer, 2012; Südhof and Rothman, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SNARE complexes are helix bundles formed by four cognate SNARE motifs, Qa, Qb, Qc, and R.
source: SNARE complexes are helix bundles formed by four cognate SNARE motifs, Qa, Qb, Qc, and R, which have been categorized based on sequence homology and the identity of characteristic polar residues in the central interaction layer (Bock et al., 2001; Fasshauer et al., 1998b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNARE complex structure, supported by citations.

claim: Exocytosis relies on ternary complexes out of one R-SNARE, one Qa-SNARE, and a specialized Qbc-SNARE with concatenated Qb and Qc motifs.
source: While prototypical SNARE complexes that drive intracellular fusion generally employ four single-pass transmembrane proteins with a single SNARE motif, exocytosis relies on ternary complexes out of one R-SNARE, one Qa-SNARE, and a specialized Qbc-SNARE with concatenated Qb and Qc motifs (Weimbs et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about exocytotic SNARE complexes, supported by citation.

claim: In neurons and neuroendocrine cells, the set of exocytotic SNAREs typically comprises synaptobrevin-2 (R), syntaxin-1A (Qa), and SNAP-25 (Qbc).
source: In neurons and neuroendocrine cells, the set of exocytotic SNAREs typically comprises synaptobrevin (syb)−2 (R), syntaxin (stx)−1A (Qa), and SNAP-25 (Qbc).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the specific SNARE proteins in neurons and neuroendocrine cells.

claim: The two SNARE motifs in Qbc proteins are connected by a 'linker' peptide, whose length varies between different isoforms.
source: The two SNARE motifs in Qbc proteins are connected by a 'linker' peptide, whose length varies between different isoforms.
evidence: This is a structural description of Qbc proteins based on established knowledge.

claim: Several Qbc isoforms are membrane-anchored by acylated cysteine residues in the N-terminal linker region.
source: Although all Qbc SNAREs lack a transmembrane domain, several isoforms are membrane-anchored by acylated cysteine residues in the N-terminal linker region.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how Qbc proteins associate with membranes.

claim: In SNAP-25a and b, a cluster of 4 cysteines forms a palmitoylation site.
source: In SNAP-25a and b, the principal isoforms in neurons and neuroendocrine cells, a cluster of 4 cysteines forms a palmitoylation site (Hess et al., 1992; Lane and Liu, 1997; Veit et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNAP-25 structure, supported by citations.

claim: SNAP-25 is efficiently acylated by members of the DHHC acyltransferase family.
source: While SNAP-25 is efficiently acylated by members of the DHHC acyltransferase family (Greaves et al., 2009; Greaves et al., 2010), not all cysteines seem to be modified in vivo (Foley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Not all cysteines in SNAP-25 seem to be modified in vivo.
source: While SNAP-25 is efficiently acylated by members of the DHHC acyltransferase family (Greaves et al., 2009; Greaves et al., 2010), not all cysteines seem to be modified in vivo (Foley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Membrane association of SNAP-25 is facilitated by stx-1A interactions, which likely promotes lipidation by membrane-bound acyltransferases.
source: Interestingly, membrane association is facilitated by stx-1A interactions, which likely promotes lipidation by membrane-bound acyltransferases (Gonelle-Gispert et al., 2000; Vogel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: A SNAP-25 linker fragment (aa 85–120) lacking both SNARE motifs can still be effectively acylated.
source: Yet, a SNAP-25 linker fragment (aa 85–120) lacking both SNARE motifs can still be effectively acylated (Gonzalo et al., 1999), likely owing to transient membrane interactions via hydrophobic and positively charged residues (Greaves et al., 2009; Weber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mutation of one or more cysteine residues results in a correlated reduction in plasma membrane localization of SNAP-25.
source: Mutation of one or more cysteine residues results in a correlated reduction in plasma membrane localization of SNAP-25 (Gonelle-Gispert et al., 2000; Nagy et al., 2008; Washbourne et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Acylation-deficient SNAP-25 mutants were inconsistently reported to be dysfunctional, to partially drive exocytosis, or to primarily change release kinetics.
source: Acylation-deficient SNAP-25 mutants were inconsistently reported to be dysfunctional (Washbourne et al., 2001), to partially drive exocytosis (Gonelle-Gispert et al., 2000), or to primarily change release kinetics (Nagy et al., 2008).
evidence: This summarizes conflicting findings from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Site-directed spin-labelling experiments indicated that the SNAP-25 linker is mostly unstructured.
source: Site-directed spin-labelling experiments indicated that the SNAP-25 linker is mostly unstructured (Margittai et al., 2001) and thus may act as a simple connector.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous experiments, supported by citation.

claim: The linker is only loosely associated with the SNARE complex, from which the N-terminal linker segment can be proteolytically cleaved.
source: This view was fostered by data that the linker is only loosely associated with the SNARE complex, from which the N-terminal linker segment can be proteolytically cleaved (Fasshauer et al., 1998a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The linker domain is dispensable for liposome fusion in vitro.
source: Moreover, the linker domain is dispensable for liposome fusion in vitro (Parlati et al., 1999)
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous in vitro experiments, supported by citation.

claim: The physical linkage of SNARE motifs seems inconsequential for secretion in cracked Botulinum toxin /E treated PC12 cells, as infusion of a toxin-resistant Qc motif can reinstate release.
source: and the physical linkage of SNARE motifs seems inconsequential for secretion in cracked Botulinum toxin (BoTn) /E treated PC12 cells, as infusion of a toxin-resistant Qc motif can reinstate release (Chen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous experiments, supported by citation.

claim: Rescue efficiency of complementing SNAP-25 fragments in cellular assays seems to strictly depend on experimental conditions.
source: However, rescue efficiency of complementing SNAP-25 fragments in cellular assays seems to strictly depend on experimental conditions, as another study reported a recovery of secretion only in permeabilized cells after initial rundown of release (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous experiments, supported by citation.

claim: Functional differences between the Qbc isoforms SNAP-25 and SNAP-23 have recently been attributed to a short sequence variation within the linker.
source: Contradicting the notion of a dispensable linker, functional differences between the Qbc isoforms SNAP-25 and SNAP-23 have recently been attributed to a short sequence variation within the linker (Nagy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: Co-expression of SN1-L and mCh-SN2 resulted in a poor reconstitution of the secretory response to a brief increase of [Ca2+]i in KO cells.
source: Strikingly, co-expression of a fragment covering SN1 and the full linker (SN1-L; aa 1–141) together with mCh-SN2 (aa 138–206) only resulted in a poor reconstitution of the secretory response to a brief increase of [Ca2+]i (~30 µM) in KO cells (Figure 1Aa,b)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 1Aa,b.

claim: Release mediated by isolated SNAP-25 fragments was kinetically delayed compared to controls expressing wildtype SNAP-25.
source: Moreover, release mediated by isolated SNAP-25 fragments under these conditions was kinetically delayed compared to controls expressing wildtype (WT) SNAP-25, as seen from a significant increase in the time constant of monoexponential fits (Figure 1Ab) of ΔCM.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 1Ab.

claim: Expression of SN25Δ26 instead of the shorter SN1-L fragment did not enhance but clearly suppress secretion.
source: To better compare our rescue data with the original results of Chen et al. (1999), we also expressed SN25Δ26 (aa 1–180) together with mCh-SN2 in KO chromaffin cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). Expression of SN25Δ26 instead of the shorter SN1-L fragment did however not enhance but clearly suppress secretion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1Ca,b), replicating a known dominant-negative action of SN25Δ26 (Sørensen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The data point to a yet unacknowledged mechanistic requirement for SNAP-25 linker continuity in secretion.
source: In sum, our data thus point to a yet unacknowledged mechanistic requirement for SNAP-25 linker continuity in secretion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on fragment complementation.

claim: No rescue of transmitter release was detected in KO cells expressing SN25 LGGS.
source: While expression of WT SNAP-25 reinstated the full secretory response upon stimulation by Ca2+-uncaging, no rescue of transmitter release was detected in KO cells expressing SN25 LGGS (Figure 1Ba,b).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 1Ba,b.

claim: Infusion of a 19 µM Ca2+-containing solution via the patch pipette for up to 5 min did not result in a recovery of secretion in cells expressing SN25 LGGS.
source: Intriguingly, we found that even infusion of a 19 µM Ca2+-containing solution via the patch pipette for up to 5 min did not result in a recovery of secretion in cells expressing SN25 LGGS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SN25 LGGS exerted a mild dominant-negative effect in WT chromaffin cells.
source: Nevertheless, SN25 LGGS exerted a mild dominant-negative effect in WT chromaffin cells, suggesting that the mutant still interacts with cognate SNARE partners via its intact SNARE motifs but fails to support exocytosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Total GFP fluorescence intensity of cells expressing SN25 LGGS was indistinguishable from WT controls.
source: Since total GFP fluorescence intensity of cells expressing SN25 LGGS was indistinguishable from WT controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), the observed secretion phenotype of SN25 LGGS cannot be simply due to insufficient expression of the mutant protein.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, used to rule out an alternative explanation.

claim: An acylation-deficient SNAP-25 mutant (SNAP-25 C84S, C85S, C90S, C92S; SN25 LN4CS) can still mediate substantial amounts of release.
source: Noteworthy, it has been reported before (Nagy et al., 2008) and is also demonstrated here (Figure 3A) that an acylation-deficient SNAP-25 mutant (SNAP-25 C84S, C85S, C90S, C92S; SN25 LN4CS) can still mediate substantial amounts of release
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3A, and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The loss of acylation and the resulting mislocalization of SN25 LGGS do not primarily account for the severe secretion deficits.
source: which excludes the possibility that the loss of acylation and the resulting mislocalization of SN25 LGGS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) primarily account for the severe secretion deficits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the phenotypes of different mutants.

claim: The native linker provides critical functional support for the fusion process, in particular in late mechanistic steps, wherein its motifs stabilize primed vesicles and facilitate fusion triggering.
source: Hence, our data suggest a mechanistic requirement for specific biophysical properties and/or special motifs of the SNAP-25 linker peptide during fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on linker substitution mutants.

claim: SN25 LGGS was still able to engage in SNARE complex formation under these conditions, which largely excludes a gross misfolding of the SNARE motifs.
source: Interestingly, our assay demonstrated that SN25 LGGS was still able to engage in SNARE complex formation under these conditions, which largely excludes a gross misfolding of the SNARE motifs (Figure 2Ab).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 2Ab, with an inference about protein structure.

claim: The assembly kinetics of SNARE complexes containing SN25 LGGS was clearly decelerated in comparison to WT controls.
source: The assembly kinetics of SNARE complexes containing SN25 LGGS was however clearly decelerated in comparison to WT controls (Figure 2Ad)
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 2Ad.

claim: Complex formation in experiments with SN25 LGGS was considerably faster than the kinetics observed for separated SN1 and SN2 motifs.
source: Yet, complex formation in experiments with SN25 LGGS was considerably faster than the kinetics observed for separated SN1 and SN2 motifs (Figure 2Ab-d), emphasizing the importance of a physical linkage of both motifs for reaction speed.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 2Ab-d, with an inference about the importance of linkage.

claim: The rate constant for the initial rapid phase of SNARE assembly was significantly decreased for SN25 LGGS in comparison to controls.
source: Fitting the kinetic profiles with a biexponential function, we found that the rate constant for the initial rapid phase of SNARE assembly was significantly decreased for SN25 LGGS in comparison to controls (Figure 2Ad).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 2Ad.

claim: Linker-less SNAP-25 fragments exhibited a strong decrease in the fast rate constant, which was accompanied by a reduction in the total amount of SNARE complexes assembled within 24 hr.
source: In case of linker-less SNAP-25 fragments, our analysis also revealed a strong decrease in the fast rate constant, which was accompanied by a reduction in the total amount of SNARE complexes assembled within 24 hr (2.19*105 ± 0.17*105 a.u., WT: 4.37*105 ± 0.52*105 a.u.; p<0.01).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claim: SNARE complexes formed by SN25 LGGS or separated SN1 and SN2 motifs exhibited a characteristic size shift (~180 kDa), which possibly suggests the formation of SNARE complex dimers.
source: SNARE complexes formed by SN25 LGGS or separated SN1 and SN2 motifs exhibited a characteristic size shift (~180 kDa; Figure 2Ab-c), which possibly suggests the formation of SNARE complex dimers.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study, shown in Figure 2Ab-c, with a speculative interpretation.

claim: Previous work by Fdez et al. (2008) has shown that two fully formed ternary complexes containing linker-less SN1/SN2 fragments can assemble into dimeric structures with attached C-terminal tips.
source: Indeed, previous work by Fdez et al. (2008) has shown that two fully formed ternary complexes containing linker-less SN1/SN2 fragments can assemble into dimeric structures with attached C-terminal tips.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: The primary structure of the SNAP-25 linker peptide likely affects the biochemical properties of SNAREpins and their propensity to dimerize.
source: Thus, the primary structure of the SNAP-25 linker peptide likely affects the biochemical properties of SNAREpins and their propensity to dimerize.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations of SNARE complex formation.

claim: SN25 LGGS bound to stx-1A at a ~ 50% lower molar ratio than WT protein.
source: Intriguingly, we found that SN25 LGGS bound to stx-1A at a ~ 50% lower molar ratio than WT protein (Figure 2Ba,b,h).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 2Ba,b,h.

claim: Earlier biochemical work demonstrated that stx-1A only interacts with truncated SNAP-25 fragments that contain the unperturbed SN1 motif.
source: Earlier biochemical work demonstrated that stx-1A only interacts with truncated SNAP-25 fragments that contain the unperturbed SN1 motif (Chapman et al., 1994), derogating the role of the linker and SN2 motif in directly binding to stx-1A H3.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: When an equimolar mix of isolated SN1 and SN2 fragments was incubated with stx-1A, SN1 was almost exclusively retained on beads.
source: When an equimolar mix of isolated SN1 and SN2 fragments was incubated with stx-1A, SN1 was almost exclusively retained on beads (Figure 2Bc,h), as expected (Chapman et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 2Bc,h, consistent with previous work.

claim: Adding the linker back to SN1 (aa 1–142; SN1-L) did not increase fragment binding, nor did it facilitate the retention of SN2.
source: Adding the linker back to SN1 (aa 1–142; SN1-L) did not increase fragment binding, nor did it facilitate the retention of SN2 (Figure 2Bd,h).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 2Bd,h.

claim: A continuous linker-SN2 fragment (aa 83–206; L-SN2) bound to immobilized GST-stx-1A in the presence of isolated SN1 motifs but not in their absence.
source: In contrast, a continuous linker-SN2 fragment (aa 83–206; L-SN2) bound to immobilized GST-stx-1A in the presence of isolated SN1 motifs (Figure 2Be,h) but not in their absence (Figure 2Bf,h).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 2Be,h and Figure 2Bf,h.

claim: The amount of retained SN1 significantly increased in the presence of L-SN2, suggesting that linker-mediated recruitment of SN2 also stabilizes the whole assembly.
source: The amount of retained SN1 also significantly increased in the presence of L-SN2, suggesting that linker-mediated recruitment of SN2 also stabilizes the whole assembly.
evidence: This is an experimental finding with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: SN2 and linker form a functional unit that likely binds to SN1:stx-1A complexes.
source: Thus, SN2 and linker form a functional unit that likely binds to SN1:stx-1A complexes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on fragment binding.

claim: The presence of the linker in either fragment combination significantly facilitated SNARE assembly over linker-less fragments.
source: We observed that the presence of the linker in either fragment combination significantly facilitated SNARE assembly over linker-less fragments, as judged by the time constants of monoexponential fits of assembly profiles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The combination of SN1/L-SN2-fragments was slightly more efficient than SN1-L/SN2 in promoting complex formation.
source: Intriguingly, the combination of SN1/L-SN2-fragments was slightly more efficient than SN1-L/SN2 in promoting complex formation, indicating that linker interactions during initial t-SNARE assembly might indeed determine overall assembly kinetics.
evidence: This is an experimental finding with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Motifs within the native SNAP-25 linker are required for normal t-SNARE interactions as well as the fast assembly of ternary SNARE complexes.
source: In summary, motifs within the native SNAP-25 linker are required for normal t-SNARE interactions as well as the fast assembly of ternary SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on linker function.

claim: The severe secretory phenotype of SN25 LGGS is probably caused by ineffective SNARE interactions that hinder complex initiation.
source: Accordingly, the severe secretory phenotype of SN25 LGGS is probably caused by ineffective SNARE interactions that hinder complex initiation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on SN25 LGGS.

claim: Expression of either SN25 LNGGS or SN25 LCGGS in KO chromaffin cells produced only small secretory responses in uncaging experiments.
source: Expression of either mutant in KO chromaffin cells produced only small secretory responses in uncaging experiments (Figure 3Aa,Ba).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3Aa,Ba.

claim: Secretion levels for both SN25 LNGGS and SN25 LCGGS clearly exceeded residual release in KO cells, indicating a partial functionality of the mutant proteins.
source: Yet, secretion levels for both mutants clearly exceeded residual release in KO cells, indicating a partial functionality of the mutant proteins.
evidence: This is an experimental finding with an inference about protein function.

claim: SN25 LNGGS caused a complete loss of the RRP component, a profound reduction in SRP size, a substantially prolonged time constant for release of SRP vesicles, a moderate decrease in sustained release, and a delay in the onset of secretion.
source: In particular, we observed a complete loss of the RRP component, a profound reduction in SRP size, a substantially prolonged time constant for release of SRP vesicles, a moderate decrease in sustained release, and a delay in the onset of secretion (Figure 3Ab).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3Ab.

claim: Substitution of the N-terminal linker segment generated a 'complex' phenotype, simultaneously altering several mechanistic aspects of the fusion process including priming, primed vesicle stability, and fusion triggering.
source: Hence, substitution of the N-terminal linker segment generated a 'complex' phenotype, simultaneously altering several mechanistic aspects of the fusion process including priming, primed vesicle stability, and fusion triggering.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on SN25 LNGGS.

claim: SN25 LNGGS lacks the palmitoylation motif and consequently exhibits a dramatically reduced plasma membrane targeting.
source: Noteworthy, SN25 LNGGS lacks the palmitoylation motif and consequently exhibits a dramatically reduced plasma membrane targeting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) despite a normal overall expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The palmitoylation-deficient mutant SN25 LN4CS, which is also not targeted to the plasma membrane, showed much milder but clearly related release deficits.
source: In comparison, the palmitoylation-deficient mutant SN25 LN4CS, which is also not targeted to the plasma membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), showed much milder but clearly related release deficits (Figure 3Aa,b), indicating that the loss of membrane association is not the sole cause of diminished transmitter release.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3Aa,b, with an inference about the cause of the phenotype.

claim: The phenotype of the C-terminal substitution mutant SN25 LCGGS appeared almost identical to the one observed for SN25 LNGGS.
source: The phenotype of the C-terminal substitution mutant SN25 LCGGS appeared almost identical to the one observed for SN25 LNGGS (Figure 3Ba; see normalized plots in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3Ba and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SN25 LCGGS strongly reduced the size of both primed vesicle pools and simultaneously increased the time constants for RRP- and SRP-mediated release in comparison to controls.
source: Our kinetic analyses showed that SN25 LCGGS strongly reduced the size of both primed vesicle pools and simultaneously increased the time constants for RRP- and SRP-mediated release in comparison to controls (Figure 3Bb).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3Bb.

claim: Secretion onset was prolonged, and sustained release was decreased for SN25 LCGGS.
source: Additionally, secretion onset was prolonged, and sustained release was decreased for SN25 LCGGS (Figure 3Bb).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3Bb.

claim: C-terminal linker substitution caused defects in priming, maintenance of primed vesicles, and triggering – very much like SN25 LNGGS.
source: Thus, C-terminal linker substitution also caused defects in priming, maintenance of primed vesicles, and triggering – very much like SN25 LNGGS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on SN25 LCGGS.

claim: Structural data suggested an interaction of nonpolar side-chains in the very C-terminal linker segment with a hydrophobic groove on the core SNARE complex.
source: As structural data suggested an interaction of nonpolar side-chains in the very C-terminal linker segment with a hydrophobic groove on the core SNARE complex (Sutton et al., 1998)
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous structural studies, supported by citation.

claim: SN25 LC4G produced a substantially smaller and slower secretory response than in controls, as indicated by a strong reduction in RRP size and an increased time constant of RRP release.
source: SN25 LC4G produced a substantially smaller and slower secretory response than in controls, as indicated by a strong reduction in RRP size and an increased time constant of RRP release (Figure 3Bb).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3Bb.

claim: Even a small substitution of four amino acids in the C-terminal linker induced a complex release phenotype that is reminiscent of the defects seen in SN25 LCGGS.
source: Hence, even this small substitution induced a complex release phenotype that is reminiscent of the defects seen in SN25 LCGGS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on SN25 LC4G.

claim: The phenotypic similarity to SN25 LCGGS became even stronger, when more residues in the very C-terminal linker segment were mutated, as demonstrated by replacing the last nine amino acids by glycine residue in SN25 LC9G.
source: The phenotypic similarity to SN25 LCGGS became even stronger, when more residues in the very C-terminal linker segment were mutated, as demonstrated by replacing the last nine amino acids by glycine residue in SN25 LC9G (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The potential core complex interaction site and the adjoining linker sequence are important for a fusion intermediate that determines the fate of the primed vesicle.
source: Clearly, the potential core complex interaction site and the adjoining linker sequence are important for a fusion intermediate that determines the fate of the primed vesicle.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on C-terminal linker mutants.

claim: All C-terminal linker mutants were normally targeted to the plasma membrane and exhibited a similar overall expression level like the WT protein in controls.
source: Note that all C-terminal linker mutants were normally targeted to the plasma membrane and exhibited a similar overall expression level like the WT protein in controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,Bb), excluding the possibility that the observed secretion deficits are due to reduced protein availability.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,Bb, used to rule out an alternative explanation.

claim: Ternary SNARE complex assembly appeared only slightly decelerated in biochemical experiments with SN25 LNGGS and SN25 LCGGS.
source: Ternary SNARE complex assembly appeared only slightly decelerated in biochemical experiments with SN25 LNGGS and SN25 LCGGS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Ca–d).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Ca–d.

claim: Biexponential fits of the kinetic profiles revealed a significantly decreased initial rate constant for SN25 LNGGS and SN25 LCGGS in comparison to controls.
source: Biexponential fits of the kinetic profiles still revealed a significantly decreased initial rate constant for SN25 LNGGS and SN25 LCGGS in comparison to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Ce,f).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Ce,f.

claim: N- and C-terminal linker regions each must contain motifs that provide additive support for SNARE assembly.
source: Thus, N- and C-terminal linker regions each must contain motifs that provide additive support for SNARE assembly.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on partial linker substitution mutants.

claim: SNARE complexes formed by SN25 LNGGS (but not SN25 LCGGS) exhibited a characteristic shift towards higher molecular mass in this assay.
source: Noteworthy, SNARE complexes formed by SN25 LNGGS (but not SN25 LCGGS) also exhibited a characteristic shift towards higher molecular mass in this assay.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Only the retention of SN25 LCGGS was significantly reduced compared to WT SNAP-25 in pulldown experiments with immobilized stx-1A.
source: Furthermore, we tested both linker substitution mutants in pulldown experiments with immobilized stx-1A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and found that exclusively the retention of SN25 LCGGS was significantly reduced compared to WT SNAP-25 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1Dd).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1Dd.

claim: Only the C-terminal linker motif substantially stabilizes t-SNARE dimers, while the contribution of the N-terminal linker region is negligible.
source: This finding highlights that only the C-terminal linker motif substantially stabilizes t-SNARE dimers, while the contribution of the N-terminal linker region is negligible.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on linker mutant binding to stx-1A.

claim: Motifs in the N-terminal as well as in the C-terminal linker segment are critical for fast, Ca2+-dependent vesicle fusion.
source: In summary, our data suggest that motifs in the N-terminal as well as in the C-terminal linker segment are critical for fast, Ca2+-dependent vesicle fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on linker mutants.

claim: Both linker segments likely stabilize late fusion intermediates in a cooperative fashion, preventing unpriming and promoting Ca2+-dependent fusion triggering.
source: Both linker segments likely stabilize late fusion intermediates in a cooperative fashion, preventing unpriming and promoting Ca2+-dependent fusion triggering.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on linker mutants.

claim: Mutation of the four acylated cysteine residues in the N-terminal linker segment (SN25 LN4CS) suffices to decelerate release kinetics and decrease apparent RRP size.
source: As mutation of the four acylated cysteine residues in the N-terminal linker segment (SN25 LN4CS) suffices to decelerate release kinetics and decrease apparent RRP size (Figure 3Aa,b; cf. Nagy et al., 2008)
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 3Aa,b, and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The palmitoylation motif is located directly downstream of SN1 in all known orthologs of SNAP-25, thus mediating membrane contacts near the C-terminal end of the assembling SNARE complex.
source: Interestingly, the palmitoylation motif is located directly downstream of SN1 in all known orthologs of SNAP-25, thus mediating membrane contacts near the C-terminal end of the assembling SNARE complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNAP-25 structure across orthologs.

claim: P-GFP-SN25 LN4CS was almost exclusively localized at the plasma membrane of infected KO cells.
source: Indeed, P-GFP-SN25 LN4CS was almost exclusively localized at the plasma membrane of infected KO cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: P-GFP-SN25 WT efficiently rescued secretion in KO chromaffin cells and even reached a slightly higher release level than typically seen in other control recordings.
source: P-GFP-SN25 WT efficiently rescued secretion in KO chromaffin cells and even reached a slightly higher release level than typically seen in other control recordings (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The increase in total secretion for P-GFP-SN25 WT might be attributed to a more pronounced membrane targeting compared to the unmodified WT protein.
source: This increase in total secretion might be attributed to a more pronounced membrane targeting compared to the unmodified WT protein.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed increase in secretion.

claim: The retargeted P-GFP-SN25 LN4CS mutant still caused secretion deficits similar to the original acylation mutant despite its high membrane expression.
source: In contrast, the retargeted P-GFP-SN25 LN4CS mutant still caused secretion deficits similar to the original acylation mutant despite its high membrane expression (Figure 4Ba,b; cf. Figure 3Aa,b).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 4Ba,b and Figure 3Aa,b.

claim: Restoration of membrane localization clearly did not abate the primary deficits in fusion triggering and pool stability.
source: Restoration of membrane localization clearly did not abate the primary deficits in fusion triggering and pool stability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on P-GFP-SN25 LN4CS.

claim: Linker acylation at a defined intramolecular position is required for efficient membrane fusion, pointing to a mechanistic role for local linker-mediated membrane contacts.
source: Hence, we conclude that linker acylation at a defined intramolecular position is required for efficient membrane fusion, pointing to a mechanistic role for local linker-mediated membrane contacts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on retargeted mutants.

claim: None of the spacer insertion mutants (SN25 shift6aa/10aa/14aaL) caused a detectable reduction in the size of the secretory burst.
source: Deviating from the secretion phenotype of SN25 LN4CS, none of these spacer insertions caused a detectable reduction in the size of the secretory burst (exemplified by SN25 shift14aaL in Figure 5Ba).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 5Ba.

claim: All spacer insertion mutants consistently induced a moderate slow-down of release, as seen in scaled plots of ΔCM traces and reflected by increased time constants of RRP and SRP-mediated secretion.
source: However, all mutants consistently induced a moderate slow-down of release, as seen in scaled plots of ΔCM traces (Figure 5Bc) and reflected by increased time constants of RRP and SRP-mediated secretion in the kinetic analysis (Figure 5Bb).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 5Bc and Figure 5Bb.

claim: A significantly prolonged latency of the secretory burst was observed in all spacer insertion mutants, further confirming deficits in fusion triggering.
source: Moreover, we observed a significantly prolonged latency of the secretory burst in all mutants that further confirmed deficits in fusion triggering (Figure 5Bb).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 5Bb.

claim: Total expression and membrane localization of the three spacer insertion mutants were indistinguishable from WT controls.
source: Since total expression and membrane localization of the three mutants were indistinguishable from WT controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,Bc), the kinetic changes cannot be due to a shortage of mutant protein on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,Bc, used to rule out an alternative explanation.

claim: The phenotype of spacer insertion mutants is not caused by increased linker length per se, as the initial linker segment can be extended by seven amino acids without functional deficits using natural insertions found in the longer N-terminal linker region of the related SNAP-23 isoform.
source: Intriguingly, the phenotype is also not caused by increased linker length per se, as the initial linker segment can be extended by seven amino acids without functional deficits using natural insertions found in the longer N-terminal linker region of the related SNAP-23 isoform (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B, used to rule out an alternative explanation.

claim: The secretory burst in SN25 shift14aaLN4CS–expressing cells was further decelerated compared to SN25 LN4CS.
source: Contrary to our expectation, however, the secretory burst in SN25 shift14aaLN4CS –expressing cells was further decelerated (Figure 5Ca), as can be well appreciated in normalized plots of ΔCM (Figure 5Cc) and is evident from a significant decrease in RRP/SRP fusion rates and the prolonged exocytotic delay in kinetic analyses (Figure 5Cb).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 5Ca, Figure 5Cc, and Figure 5Cb.

claim: The substantially aggravated phenotype of SN25 shift14aaLN4CS in combination with the generally mild phenotypes of uncoupling spacer insertion mutants clearly argue against a prominent contribution of the linker to SNARE force transfer.
source: The substantially aggravated phenotype of SN25 shift14aaLN4CS in combination with the generally mild phenotypes of uncoupling spacer insertion mutants clearly argue against a prominent contribution of the linker to SNARE force transfer.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on spacer insertion mutants.

claim: The membrane interactions of the acyl anchors near the C-terminal end of the core complex must be mechanistically important for efficient fusion initiation and likely promote a favorable membrane configuration for merger.
source: Still, given the pronounced kinetic phenotype of the non-palmitoylated SN25 LN4CS mutant and its retargeted P-GFP-SN25 LN4CS variant, the membrane interactions of the acyl anchors near the C-terminal end of the core complex must be mechanistically important for efficient fusion initiation and likely promote a favorable membrane configuration for merger.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on acylation mutants.

claim: The acerbated release deficits of SN25 shift14aaLN4CS highlight acylation-independent functions of the N-terminal linker in fusion triggering, possibly involving additional lipid or protein interactions.
source: The acerbated release deficits of SN25 shift14aaLN4CS also highlight acylation-independent functions of the N-terminal linker in fusion triggering, possibly involving additional lipid or protein interactions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on SN25 shift14aaLN4CS.

claim: Work by Weber et al. (2017) recently suggested that the N-terminal linker motif mediates transient membrane contacts via electrostatic interactions between lysine side-chains and phospholipid head groups.
source: Work by Weber et al. (2017) recently suggested that the N-terminal linker motif mediates transient membrane contacts via electrostatic interactions between lysine side-chains and phospholipid head groups.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: Substitution of five lysine residues in the N-terminal linker region of SN25 LN4CS very slightly decelerated secretion in comparison to SN25 LN4CS.
source: Substitution of the lysine residues very slightly decelerated secretion in comparison to SN25 LN4CS, as indicated by an increased time constant of RRP release (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The lysine residues contribute to the linker:lipid interactions that facilitate Ca2+-dependent fusion triggering.
source: Since no difference in overall expression or membrane targeting of SN25 LN5KA,4CS compared to SN25 LN4CS was noticeable (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,Ba), we conclude that the lysine residues contribute to the linker:lipid interactions that facilitate Ca2+-dependent fusion triggering.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on SN25 LN5KA,4CS.

claim: The role of the lysine residues in the linker:membrane interface is probably more pronounced within the intact acylated linker but would be difficult to study due to an involvement in the acylation process.
source: Noteworthy, the role of the lysine residues in the linker:membrane interface is probably more pronounced within the intact acylated linker but would be difficult to study due to an involvement in the acylation process (Weber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation about the role of lysine residues, with a citation to previous work.

claim: The N-terminal linker region engages in different interactions with the plasma membrane that are important for late mechanistic steps of the fusion process.
source: In sum, our data suggest that the N-terminal linker region engages in different interactions with the plasma membrane that are important for late mechanistic steps of the fusion process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on N-terminal linker mutants.

claim: Linker:membrane contacts may only play a limited role in force transfer, but the data hint at a mechanistic scenario, in which acyl anchors and local electrostatic membrane interactions cooperatively establish a suitable membrane configuration for fusion triggering.
source: While these linker:membrane contacts may only play a limited role in force transfer, our results hint at a mechanistic scenario, in which acyl anchors and local electrostatic membrane interactions cooperatively establish a suitable membrane configuration for fusion triggering.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on linker mutants.

claim: SN25 LN4CS significantly prolonged the pre-spike signal (PS) but left the main spike signal unperturbed.
source: In accord with Nagy et al., 2008, we found that SN25 LN4CS significantly prolonged the pre-spike signal (PS) (Figure 6C) but left the main spike signal unperturbed (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6B, consistent with previous work.

claim: The N-terminal substitution mutant SN25 LNGGS affected the PS as well as the kinetics of the main spike.
source: Interestingly, the N-terminal substitution mutant SN25 LNGGS affected the PS as well as the kinetics of the main spike: Similar to SN25 LN4CS, the PS was significantly prolonged (Figure 6Cc), exhibiting reduced amplitudes (Figure 6Ca,b) and diminished current fluctuations (Figure 6Ce,f). Additionally, rise time and half width of the main spike signal were significantly increased (Figure 6Bc,d), while the total charge remained unchanged (Figure 6Ba).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 6.

claim: The effects on main spike waveform induced by SN25 LNGGS clearly indicate that the N-terminal linker region surrounding the cysteine cluster participates in the control of late fusion pore expansion.
source: The effects on main spike waveform induced by SN25 LNGGS clearly indicate that the N-terminal linker region surrounding the cysteine cluster participates in the control of late fusion pore expansion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on SN25 LNGGS.

claim: Removal of the flanking lysine residues in SN25 LN5KA,4CS was sufficient to delay main spike kinetics, establishing a congruent phenotype to SN25 LNGGS.
source: Confirming this notion, removal of the flanking lysine residues in SN25 LN5KA,4CS was sufficient to delay main spike kinetics, establishing a congruent phenotype to SN25 LNGGS (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 6B–C.

claim: Similar deficits in early and late fusion pore behavior were observed for SN25 shift14aaL.
source: Moreover, similar deficits in early and late fusion pore behavior were observed for SN25 shift14aaL (Figure 6B–C), demonstrating that a displacement of the palmitoylation motif effectively disturbs the linker-mediated support of pore dilation.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 6B–C, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The lack of kinetic alterations in cells expressing the C-terminal substitution mutant SN25 LCGGS suggests that fusion pore regulation is selectively tied to the N-terminal linker region.
source: The lack of kinetic alterations in cells expressing the C-terminal substitution mutant SN25 LCGGS (Figure 6B–C) finally suggests that fusion pore regulation is selectively tied to the N-terminal linker region.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 6B–C, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Lipid interplay of the N-terminal linker segment with the neck of the fusion pore governs the behavior of the pore from its initial opening to the final stages of membrane merger.
source: Hence, our data suggest that lipid interplay of the N-terminal linker segment with the neck of the fusion pore governs the behavior of the pore from its initial opening to the final stages of membrane merger.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on fusion pore kinetics.

claim: Application of short-chain alcohols was reported to facilitate hemifusion/fusion of liposomes in reduced protein-free systems by altering membrane properties.
source: Application of short-chain alcohols was reported to facilitate hemifusion/fusion of liposomes in reduced protein-free systems by altering membrane properties (Chanturiya et al., 1999; Paxman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citations.

claim: MeOH infusion into SNAP-25 WT-expressing KO cells mildly increased total secretion (+25%) by strengthening the SRP component.
source: Indeed, MeOH infusion into SNAP-25 WT-expressing KO cells mildly increased total secretion (+25%) by strengthening the SRP component (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 7.

claim: The same MeOH treatment resulted in a profound recovery of the secretory burst in SN25 LNGGS–expressing KO cells, basically doubling total secretion.
source: The very same treatment resulted in a profound recovery of the secretory burst in SN25 LNGGS–expressing KO cells, basically doubling total secretion (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The restoration of release by MeOH suggests that the alcohol-induced changes in lipid properties can partially compensate for the loss of linker:membrane interactions.
source: The restoration of release suggests that the alcohol-induced changes in lipid properties can partially compensate for the loss of linker:membrane interactions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on MeOH treatment.

claim: MeOH treatment of SN25 LNGGS–expressing KO cells selectively reconstituted primed vesicle pools and the sustained release component, leaving release rates unchanged.
source: Interestingly, MeOH treatment of SN25 LNGGS–expressing KO cells selectively reconstituted primed vesicle pools and the sustained release component, leaving release rates unchanged (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The data primarily point to a MeOH-induced recovery of priming and priming stability.
source: Thus, our data primarily point to a MeOH-induced recovery of priming and priming stability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on MeOH treatment.

claim: Short-chain alcohols likely affect hydration repulsion, and it stands to reason that MeOH compensates for an insufficient local shielding of the plasma membrane surface caused by elimination of local linker:lipid interactions.
source: As short-chain alcohols likely affect hydration repulsion (Ly and Longo, 2004; Paxman et al., 2017), it stands to reason that MeOH compensates for an insufficient local shielding of the plasma membrane surface caused by elimination of local linker:lipid interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the MeOH rescue effect, supported by citations.

claim: Curvature-inducing lipids are known to either facilitate or inhibit membrane merger in the context of various model systems, including liposome fusion and virus-mediated membrane fusion.
source: Curvature-inducing lipids are known to either facilitate or inhibit membrane merger in the context of various model systems, including liposome fusion and virus-mediated membrane fusion (Chernomordik and Kozlov, 2003; Melia et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Cone-shaped lipids support the highly-bent stalk intermediate during fast Ca2+-triggered fusion of secretory vesicles.
source: As it was reported that cone-shaped lipids support the highly-bent stalk intermediate during fast Ca2+-triggered fusion of secretory vesicles (Churchward et al., 2008)
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: OA infusion in control experiments induced a ~ 50% gain in total capacitance over 2 min compared to vehicle-treated cells.
source: OA infusion in these control experiments induced a ~ 50% gain in total capacitance over 2 min compared to vehicle-treated cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Infusion of SN25 LNGGS–expressing KO with OA almost tripled the membrane capacitance increase seen within 2 min.
source: In stark contrast, infusion of SN25 LNGGS–expressing KO with OA almost tripled the membrane capacitance increase seen within 2 min (Figure 8A), indicating that the facilitating action of OA can in part accommodate for the loss of N-terminal linker interactions.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 8A, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The membrane anchor and flanking linker sequences support a critical lipidic fusion intermediate that is sensitive to curvature-inducing agents.
source: Hence, we propose that the membrane anchor and flanking linker sequences support a critical lipidic fusion intermediate that is sensitive to curvature-inducing agents.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on OA treatment.

claim: Curvature-perturbing lipids have been shown to affect the life-time of the nascent fusion pore.
source: As curvature-perturbing lipids have been shown to affect the life-time of the nascent fusion pore (Zhang and Jackson, 2010)
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: In control experiments with SNAP-25 WT-expressing cells, application of OA resulted in a clear acceleration of PS and main spike waveform.
source: In control experiments with SNAP-25 WT-expressing cells, application of OA resulted in a clear acceleration of PS and main spike waveform, as reflected by a decreased rise time and half width (Figure 8Bc,d), an increased spike amplitude (Figure 8Bb), and a shortening of PSs (Figure 8Ca).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 8Bc,d, Figure 8Bb, and Figure 8Ca.

claim: A similar kinetic speed-up of spike kinetics was also observed, when OA was introduced into SN25 LNGGS–expressing KO cells, compensating for all decelerating effects of the linker mutation on PS and main spike signals.
source: A similar kinetic speed-up of spike kinetics was also observed, when OA was introduced into SN25 LNGGS–expressing KO cells (Figure 8B,C), in result compensating for all decelerating effects of the linker mutation on PS and main spike signals.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: The full reversal of the kinetic deficits of SN25 LNGGS suggests that linker-mediated membrane interactions and OA both influence the same mechanistic determinant of pore evolution.
source: The full reversal of the kinetic deficits of SN25 LNGGS suggests that linker-mediated membrane interactions and OA both influence the same mechanistic determinant of pore evolution.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on OA treatment.

claim: The N-terminal lipid contacts could directly regulate pore expansion by altering membrane curvature near the fusion pore neck.
source: Thus, our data suggest the possibility that the N-terminal lipid contacts could directly regulate pore expansion by altering membrane curvature near the fusion pore neck.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the role of N-terminal linker interactions.
